title: What is the difference between static binding (compile-time: private/static/final methods, overloaded resolution on reference type) and dynamic binding (runtime: overridden instance methods, resolved on actual object type via vtable), and why does Parent p = new Child(); p.method() call Child's version?
shortTitle: What is static binding vs dynamic binding?
keyPoints: Static binding resolves method calls at compile time based on the reference type (early binding)
Dynamic binding resolves method calls at runtime based on the actual object type via the vtable (late binding)
Static binding is used for private, static, final methods and overloaded method resolution
Dynamic binding is used for overridden instance methods, enabling runtime polymorphism
Parent p = new Child(); p.method() calls Child's version because the JVM dispatches via the vtable at runtime
Static binding is faster (no vtable lookup), dynamic binding enables polymorphism

s1_definition.oneliner: Static binding resolves at compile time using the reference type, for private, static, final, and overloaded methods. Dynamic binding resolves at runtime using the actual object type via the vtable, for overridden instance methods.
s1_definition.profdef:
Two binding mechanisms determine which method code runs when a call is made.

- **Static binding** (early binding): resolved at compile time. The compiler looks at the reference type and binds directly. Used for `private` methods (not inherited, no override), `static` methods (class-level, no vtable), `final` methods (sealed, no override), and overloaded methods (compiler picks signature by argument types).
- **Dynamic binding** (late binding): resolved at runtime. The JVM looks at the actual object type in the heap and dispatches via the virtual method table (vtable). Used for overridden instance methods.
- `Parent p = new Child(); p.method()` calls Child's version because the JVM checks `p`'s actual type (Child) at runtime, not the variable type (Parent).
- Static binding is faster (no vtable lookup). Dynamic binding enables polymorphism.
s1_definition.analogy: Static binding: the bank's directory at National Bank of India says for accounts, go to Counter 1. You look at the directory (compile time) and go there. It does not matter who is sitting at Counter 1 today. Dynamic binding: you call customer service and say I need help with my account. The system checks your actual account type (savings or current) at that moment and routes you to the right specialist. The routing happens at the moment of the call (runtime), not when the phone system was installed (compile time).

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Account ref = new SavingsAccount();

  STATIC BINDING                    DYNAMIC BINDING
  (compile-time)                    (runtime)
  ┌────────────────────┐           ┌────────────────────┐
  │ ref.getPolicy()     │           │ ref.getDescription()│
  │ ref.getAccountId()  │           │                    │
  │ ref.callAudit()     │           │ JVM at runtime:    │
  │                     │           │ actual type?        │
  │ Compiler binds to   │           │ SavingsAccount     │
  │ Account at compile  │           │      │             │
  │ time.               │           │      ▼             │
  │                     │           │ vtable lookup      │
  │ No vtable lookup.   │           │      │             │
  │ Faster.             │           │      ▼             │
  │                     │           │ SavingsAccount     │
  │                     │           │ .getDescription()  │
  └────────────────────┘           └────────────────────┘

  METHOD TYPE -> BINDING
  private    -> static  (invokespecial)
  static     -> static  (invokestatic)
  final      -> static  (invokevirtual, but JVM can inline)
  overloaded -> static  (compiler picks signature)
  overridden -> dynamic (invokevirtual, vtable dispatch)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Static binding resolves method calls at compile time. The compiler looks at the reference type and binds directly. Used for private methods (not inherited, no vtable entry), static methods (class-level, no vtable), final methods (sealed, JVM can inline), and overloaded methods (compiler picks signature by argument types). Dynamic binding resolves at runtime. The JVM looks at the actual object type in the heap and dispatches via the vtable. Used for overridden instance methods, which is the mechanism behind runtime polymorphism.

Parent p = new Child(); p.method() calls Child's version because the compiler generates invokevirtual Parent.method() (valid: Parent has the method). At runtime, the JVM checks p's actual object (Child), looks up Child's vtable, finds Child.method(), and calls it. The variable type (Parent) determined compile-time validity. The actual type (Child) determined runtime dispatch. This is why polymorphism works, and why static methods do not exhibit polymorphism (they use invokestatic which binds to the class at compile time, ignoring the actual object).

Remember one sentence: static binding resolves at compile time by reference type (private, static, final, overloaded), dynamic binding resolves at runtime by actual object type (overridden instance methods via vtable), and this is why p.method() calls Child's version when p holds a Child object.
